title: session.token.v1: a token scoped to one session
description: A session token lets an engine that runs inside one session ask the daemon for a few things about that session and the sessions it starts, and nothing else. The token itself ($defs/token) is opaque: a client never parses it. It never appears in a record or an event; every closed record in this folder refuses a field that would hold one. The record at the root is the GRANT the daemon keeps for a token: it is PRIVATE, never sent to any client, and it holds the token's SHA-256, never the token. verbs lists what the token may call, each one of the delegable methods ($defs/delegable_method); approval.open, approval.answer and every method that needs 'manage' can never be delegated, so an engine can never approve its own request. A session principal's id is the session's id. NOT DEFINED HERE: how a token is presented and admitted on the socket. Today a peer inside a run unit is closed at accept, before any frame is read; admitting one with a token needs its own bounded admission capacity, so that it cannot take the connections kept for Stop before it has shown a valid token. That is a later design of the lanes that own the socket and Stop.

token_id.description: A label for the grant, safe to log. It is not the token and cannot be turned into it.

expires_at.description: null means the token lasts as long as its session. A token never outlives its session.

revoked_at.description: When the token was revoked, or null. A revoked token is refused at once.

token.description: The token as it travels: 'rst1_' and 43 characters of URL-safe base64 (32 random bytes). The prefix lets a secret scanner recognise one. Opaque: nothing is to be read out of it.

delegable_method.description: PROVISIONAL, for the lanes that own scopes and delegation to confirm. The methods a session token may be granted. With one, an engine can start a child session, send it work, watch it, and stop its own subtree.
